opus-5.5.text:
I think it's very likely, and in many ways it's already happening. The core problem in robot learning is data. Language models had the whole internet; we don't have an internet of robot actions. Teleoperation data is expensive and slow to collect, and it doesn't scale the way we'd like. Video, especially human video, is the closest thing we have to an internet-scale source of physical interaction. It contains a huge amount of information about how the world works: how objects move, how people use tools, what a reasonable sequence of steps looks like for a task.

So I see video becoming a very important foundation, but I'd be careful about the word "reliant." Video gives you the "what" and some of the "why," but it's missing a lot of the "how" for a robot. You don't get forces, you don't get tactile feedback, and there's an embodiment gap: a human hand isn't a parallel-jaw gripper, and the camera viewpoint is rarely the robot's. Watching someone crack an egg doesn't tell you how hard to squeeze.

The picture I find most compelling is layered. Use large amounts of video, through world models, video prediction, or learning latent actions, to build priors about physics, object affordances, and task structure. Then ground those priors with a much smaller amount of robot-specific data, maybe from teleoperation, maybe from wearable devices that capture human demonstrations in a more robot-friendly form, plus simulation and the robot's own experience. The video gives you breadth. The embodied data gives you precision and closes the loop.

There's also an interesting question about whether video world models can serve as simulators: you imagine the outcome of an action, evaluate it, and plan. That's exciting, but these models still hallucinate physics in subtle ways, and in manipulation small errors matter a lot. So I'm optimistic but not naive. Video will be a central ingredient, maybe the largest one by volume, but I don't think it will be the whole recipe. The field's progress will come from figuring out how to bridge watching and doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes video as informative about interaction but incomplete for robot learning, citing missing forces and tactile feedback and the embodiment gap.

r002.rationale: It contrasts scalable, internet-scale video with costly, slower robot-specific data that provides precision, framing data sources as a breadth-versus-precision tradeoff.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because video is really the one modality where we have this almost unlimited supply of data about how the physical world works. If you look at what happened in language, scale was the thing that unlocked everything, and robotics has never had that. We can't just scrape the internet for robot trajectories. So it's very natural that people look at video and say, okay, this is our internet-scale data source.

And I do think there's real signal there. Videos of humans doing things encode a lot of what we care about: how objects move, how tasks decompose into steps, what affordances look like, what a reasonable sequence of actions is to make a sandwich or open a drawer. Video prediction models, world models trained on video, these can give you a kind of intuitive physics and a prior over plausible futures that's very hard to get from a few hundred teleoperation demos in a lab.

But I'm also somewhat cautious about going all in on it, for a couple of reasons. The first is that video doesn't come with actions. You see the outcome, you see the motion, but you don't see the torques, the contact forces, the fine-grained control decisions that actually made it happen. And a lot of what makes manipulation hard lives exactly in that gap. Grasping a slippery cup, inserting a connector, anything contact-rich, those are things where the pixels look almost identical whether you succeed or fail, and the difference is in the force profile. So if your model's understanding of the world is entirely visual, it may be very good at knowing what should happen and quite bad at making it happen.

The second concern is the embodiment gap. Most of the video out there is of humans, and human hands are not robot grippers. You can learn high-level structure, but you still need some bridge that grounds that into a specific robot's kinematics and sensors. And that bridge usually requires real robot data, which brings you back to the same bottleneck, just with a smaller hole to fill.

So my view is that video is going to be a huge part of the picture, probably the backbone for the perception and planning side, the part that tells the robot what the world is and what a good plan looks like. But I'd be nervous if the field treated it as the whole answer. I think the systems that actually work are going to be hybrid: video-pretrained representations, combined with real interaction data, simulation, maybe proprioceptive and tactile sensing, and then some mechanism for the robot to keep learning from its own experience. Video gets you most of the way to understanding, and then you need something else for the last bit, which is actually acting.

r001.rationale: The response says video shows outcomes and motion but omits actions, torques, and contact forces, making it an incomplete measurement for learning manipulation.

r002.rationale: It contrasts video’s internet-scale supply with real robot data’s richer action and force information, framing scalability against measurement fidelity.

astra-6.text:
I think video could play a really important role. It captures a lot of what we want robots to understand: how people interact with objects, how a task progresses, and what a successful outcome looks like. If we can learn those things from video, we don’t have to collect every example on a robot, which is expensive and difficult to scale.

But there’s a gap between watching something and knowing how to do it. You can watch someone open a drawer, but you don’t necessarily know how much force they applied or what they felt when it got stuck. And a robot’s body is different from a human’s, so it can’t simply copy the motion.

So I can imagine models becoming heavily reliant on video for learning about the world and about tasks. But they still need experience acting in the world to connect that understanding to control. The interesting question is how much of that foundation we can get from video, and how little robot interaction we need to make it useful.

r001.rationale: The response presents video as useful but incomplete: it may show task progress and outcomes, yet misses force and tactile feedback and cannot be directly copied to a robot.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts video’s scalability with its limited fidelity for learning control, and notes that robot data is expensive and difficult to scale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think video is going to play a very important role. There’s so much information in video about how the world works—how objects move, how people interact with them, and what a successful task looks like. It would be hard to ignore that as a source of data for robot learning.

But there’s a gap between watching something happen and knowing how to make it happen. In a video, you don’t necessarily observe the forces, the contact, or the actions that produced a motion. And a human hand has different capabilities from a robot gripper. So learning from video doesn’t automatically give you a policy that you can put on a robot.

My view is that video can provide a lot of the prior knowledge, but robots still need experience interacting with the world to ground that knowledge in their own actions. The interesting question is how much physical experience you need, and how effectively you can use it to turn what the model has seen into something the robot can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says video reveals useful information but may omit forces, contact, and the actions that produced motion, describing it as an incomplete measurement for robot learning.

r002.rationale: It contrasts learning from video with robots’ need for physical interaction, but does not frame the data-source choice as a tradeoff between measurement fidelity and scalability.
